cues.text: Chapter two: Requirements engineering.
Let us begin with the most basic distinction in this chapter.
Functional requirements define what the system shall do.
Nonfunctional requirements, which are also called quality requirements, define how well the system operates, or they define constraints on it.
So one kind says what the system does, and the other says how well it does it, or within what limits.
Here is an example of each.
"Allow password reset through email" is a functional requirement.
It describes a thing the system shall do.
Now compare it with this statement: "95% of successful reset requests complete within two seconds under defined load." That is a measurable performance requirement.
Notice the pieces that make it measurable: a percentage, which is ninety-five percent; a time limit of two seconds; and a stated condition, which is the defined load.
Without those, "fast" would just be an opinion.
Security is interesting because it can appear on both sides.
It can be expressed as functional controls, for example, require MFA, meaning multi-factor authentication.
And it can also be expressed as quality constraints.
Now the source also separates requirements by level.
Business requirements describe why.
They explain the reason the work is being done.
User requirements describe needs, meaning what the users need.
And system requirements refine behaviour, taking those needs and making the expected behaviour of the system more precise.
Next, how do we find requirements, and what do we do with them?
We elicit them.
Elicit means to draw out.
The source lists these techniques: interviews, workshops, observation, surveys, document analysis, prototypes, and existing analytics.
After eliciting, the activities continue in this order: analyse conflicts, prioritise, document, validate, and manage changes.
What makes a requirement good?
The source gives six qualities.
A good requirement is clear, consistent, feasible, testable, traceable, and necessary.
Now we meet a pair of terms that students often confuse.
Verification checks conformity to specified requirements.
In other words, did we build it according to what was specified?
Validation checks whether the right product satisfies real user and business needs.
So verification looks back at the specification, while validation looks at the real needs of users and the business.
The source adds a warning: stakeholder sign-off is weak if nobody actually reviews the workflow.
A signature on its own proves little.
To make validation real, the source recommends demonstrations, acceptance tests, and traceability.
Let us move to how requirements are written down.
A user story follows a pattern.

Here is the example: "As a dispatcher, I want to see delayed shipments so that I can intervene." There is a role, which is the dispatcher; a want, which is to see delayed shipments; and a reason, which is so that they can intervene.
Acceptance criteria then specify observable outcomes.
The example reads: given an overdue shipment, when the dispatcher views the queue, then it is flagged with the correct timestamp and authorised details.
See the structure: given a starting situation, when an action happens, then an observable result follows.
Notice also that the result mentions authorised details, so access rights are part of the outcome.
A use case is a different format.
It documents the actor, the goal, the normal flow, alternatives, and exceptions.
For more formal documentation, an SRS or FRD offers more formal structure.
And the backlog is an evolving ordered list, so it changes over time, but always has an order.
Finally, prioritisation.
MoSCoW is a scheme with four categories.
Must have means essential.
Should have means important but deferrable.
Could have means desirable.
And Won't have this time means exactly that: not included in this round.
When prioritising, consider value, risk, dependency, and capacity.
Then there is estimation.
Story points estimate relative effort, complexity, and uncertainty.
They are not fixed hours.
Now follow the capacity example carefully.
Suppose capacity is 20 points.
The must items are 8 plus 5, which is 13.
A should item of 5 fits, bringing the total to 18.
A could item of 3 does not fit, because 18 plus 3 is 21, which exceeds 20.
Then change happens.
If an urgent must item adds 4, the total mandatory work becomes 17, that is 13 plus 4.
The source's guidance is clear: replan the lower priority items instead of silently exceeding capacity.
The team should not quietly overload itself; it should make an explicit decision about what moves.
